Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time

Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time

开发工具 作者 xbmcuser 热度 686 回复 437 2026/10/17 22:01
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Solar and wind are increasingly outpacing nuclear power globally, with solar generation surpassing nuclear for the first time in 2025, according to WNISR 2026. The report highlights nuclear’s slow growth, lengthy construction timelines and limited small modular reactor deployment, contrasting them with rapid renewables and battery expansion. The World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, overseen by French nuclear energy consultant Mycle Schneider, shows that wind power alone surpassed nuclear generation on a monthly basis in March 2025, followed by solar in April – the first time global monthly solar generation exceeded nuclear output.
  • From March 2025 through June 2026, either solar or wind individually generated more electricity than nuclear every month. In March, April and May 2026, both technologies independently surpassed nuclear generation.

philipkglass 2026/10/17 22:29
Note that this is actual generated terawatt hours. Nuclear power has a substantially higher capacity factor, but solar has been growing so rapidly that it has taken the lead on generated output too. Wind is just about to surpass nuclear generation also, though solar is racing ahead much faster. The next big milestone, not to be reached for several years at the present rate, would be solar generation overtaking hydroelectric generation. You can see data up through 2025 here:

https://ourworldindata.org/electricity-mix

Even though solar power has been a significant part of the energy conversation for decades, the majority of solar growth is very recent. Nuclear power generated 2762 TWh in 2021, when solar generated 1054 TWh. Solar power generated 2779 TWh in 2025.

Denmark's power generation from wind is around 20TWh/year, Norway hydro 140 TWh/year, and Swedish nuclear 50 TWh/year.

defrost 2026/10/18 12:24
As a snapshot in time, yes. The arc through is far more interesting.

Worthy of note for any readers new to this, electricity generation alone (which this figure is) is but a subset of energy consumption (fuel for transport, energy usage in industry) overall. Further not all human origin greenhouse gases come from energy consumption - coal and other fossil carbon sources are used as raw materials in industry (steel, fertiliser, etc) via processes that bind some of that fossil carbon away from the atmosphere and release a portion to the atmosphere as by product.

There's still work to be done on reduction of fossil carbon source extraction, CO2 capture from industrial processes, and direct CO2 capture from free atmosphere to mitigate the risks of over insulation for future generations.
